children: JetBlue sought to calm jittery investors Monday with a message that the airline's turnaround strategy is working and it can ride out turbulence from high fuel prices.

Shares had been in free fall ahead of the airline's third-quarter results, as investors fretted over the company's viability. The airline's stock tumbled close to 10% Monday to $2.37, closing at an all-time low for the third consecutive trading session.

But the stock gained 9.7% in extended trading after JetBlue reported quarterly results a day early that showed revenue growth. It also affirmed an earlier pledge to turn an operating profit next year.
"I'm very encouraged by the progress we made in the third quarter," Chief Executive Joanna Geraghty said in a statement.

JetBlue's third-quarter loss of $257 million, or 68 cents a share, was steeper than the year-earlier period. But the airline said it was able to cover more of its fuel expense through higher fares than expected. And its operating margins, while still negative, are improving.

The Wall Street Journal reported Friday that a group of JetBlue's senior creditors hired a financial adviser and law firm — steps creditors typically take when they perceive a risk that the company they have lent money to might not be able to fully repay them on schedule. JetBlue's bonds also traded down sharply last week.

High fuel prices are squeezing airlines' profit margins this year, and several are on track to lose money. Even though carriers have largely been able to raise fares without denting travel demand, investors fear JetBlue is running out of time to fix itself.
JetBlue faced challenges even before the start of the Iran war earlier this year caused fuel prices to soar. It hasn't turned an annual profit since before the Covid-19 pandemic.

As a smaller carrier, it has struggled to go up against the behemoths that dominate the U.S. airline industry. Its efforts to find a way around that problem — striking up an alliance with American Airlines and then trying to buy Spirit Airlines — were both struck down by federal judges as being anticompetitive.
In recent years the airline has scaled back its route network, jettisoning money-losing flights to focus on its core business serving East Coast leisure destinations.

It is also going after upscale fliers with new offerings, opening its first airport lounges in New York and Boston. Earlier this month, it started selling tickets for its new domestic first-class section. And it has homed in on Fort Lauderdale, Fla., taking advantage of the shutdown of Spirit Airlines to continue its expansion in the popular vacation spot.

While JetBlue took on more debt while its new strategy got under way, the airline said it ended the third quarter with $2.2 billion of liquidity. Chief Financial Officer Ursula Hurley said Monday that JetBlue has "the liquidity and financing options to create a strong bridge" to reach its 2028 financial targets.

"With fuel spiking and profitability pushed further out, a successful outcome has become harder," Melius Research analyst Conor Cunningham wrote Monday ahead of the results. Still, "a Chapter 11 filing is not a foregone conclusion."
